docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
invoke-tasklib is a reusable library of Invoke tasks shared across Python projects. Instead of copy-pasting the same tasks.py boilerplate (formatting, linting, type-checking, testing, environment setup, releasing, and documentation) into every repository, a project imports one namespace and gets a consistent set of invoke commands.

Quick Links:

  • Get Started
  • User Guide
  • Config
  • Troubleshooting

docs.title: Why invoke-tasklib?
docs.text:
Most Python projects end up with a tasks.py that wraps the same handful of tools: ruff, ty, pytest, docformatter, uv, mike. Keeping those wrappers in sync across many repositories is tedious, and small inconsistencies (a missing --xdoctest flag, a different coverage flag) creep in over time.

invoke-tasklib centralizes these tasks in one importable package:

from invoke_tasklib import ns

invoke --list

A single invoke.yaml at the project root configures the package name and, optionally, the paths used by the tasks:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

See the user guide for the full config schema.

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text: We highly recommend installing invoke-tasklib in a virtual environment to avoid dependency conflicts.

docs.title: Using uv (recommended)
docs.text:
uv is a fast Python package installer and resolver:

uv add --dev invoke-tasklib

docs.title: Using pip
docs.text:
Alternatively, you can use pip:

pip install invoke-tasklib

docs.title: Setting up a project
docs.text:
Starting from a typical project layout:

my_package/
├── src/
│   └── my_package/
│       └── __init__.py
├── tests/
│   └── unit/
├── pyproject.toml

docs.title: 1. Add a tasks.py
docs.text:
Add a tasks.py at the root of your project that imports the shared namespace:

# tasks.py
from invoke_tasklib import ns

docs.title: 2. Add an invoke.yaml
docs.text:
Add an invoke.yaml at the root of your project with, at minimum, the package name:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text:
To install invoke-tasklib from source, you can follow the steps below.

First, clone the git repository:

git clone git@github.com:durandtibo/invoke-tasklib.git
cd invoke-tasklib

Note: invoke-tasklib requires Python 3.11 or higher.

It is recommended to create a virtual environment (this step is optional):

uv venv --clear
source .venv/bin/activate

Then, install the project in editable mode along with its development dependencies:

uv sync --group dev

Finally, you can test the installation by running the unit tests:

python -m pytest tests/

docs.title: 'tasklib.package.name' must be set in invoke.yaml
docs.text:
Almost every task reads the config, which requires tasklib.package.name. An invalid config is reported with this one-line message and the exit code 2. Add an invoke.yaml at your project root (next to tasks.py) with at least:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

See Get Started and Config for the full schema.

docs.title: 'ruff' was not found on the PATH
docs.text:
Before running a command, the tasks check that its program (ruff, ty, uv, mike, ...) is on the PATH and exit with code 127 if it is not. Install the project tools with invoke env.install (the dev group has the linters and test tools, the docs group has mike) or activate the virtual environment that has them.

The hint depends on the program: uv points to its installation page (env.install itself needs it), shellcheck and shfmt to the system package manager, and codespell to the project dependencies. Every command of a pipeline is checked, and so is the module of python -m <module> (for example pytest), which is reported as The Python module 'pytest' is not installed for ... instead of Python's own No module named.

docs.title: invoke: command not found after installing
docs.text:
invoke-tasklib depends on invoke, but installing a library into a virtual environment does not always put its console scripts on PATH the way you expect. Make sure:

  • Your virtual environment is activated (source .venv/bin/activate), or
  • You run it via uv run invoke ..., or
  • invoke itself is installed as a tool (uv tool install invoke). Note that env.create-venv installs invoke into the new .venv, not as a tool.

docs.title: invoke --list shows no tasks / ns is empty
docs.text:
Check that tasks.py actually imports and exposes ns:

# tasks.py
from invoke_tasklib import ns

Invoke discovers tasks from a module-level ns (or namespace) variable in tasks.py; if you renamed the import or wrapped it, Invoke won't find it.

docs.title: A task fails with "command not found" (ruff, ty, shellcheck, ...)
docs.text:
invoke-tasklib tasks are wrappers around external CLI tools — it does not vendor them. Install the missing tool, either directly or via your project's dependency groups:

invoke env.install                  # installs dev deps: ruff, ty, pytest, ...
invoke env.install --groups dev,docs  # additionally installs mike

shellcheck and shfmt are not Python packages; install them with your system package manager (e.g. brew install shellcheck shfmt on macOS) — see the Format page. The full external-tool matrix is in the User Guide overview.

docs.title: doc.publish-latest fails with No version tag found
docs.text:
doc.publish-latest reads the last git tag that looks like v1.2.3. Create a release tag (and fetch the tags in CI: git fetch --tags), or skip the tag lookup by passing the version:

invoke doc.publish-latest --version 1.2

docs.title: doc.publish-latest fails with Refusing to publish ... as latest
docs.text:
A newer version of the docs is already published, so publishing this one would move latest backwards. Pass --force if that is what you want.

See Doc.

docs.title: release.pypi fails to authenticate
docs.text:
release.pypi passes the PYPI_TOKEN (or UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN) environment variable to uv publish and stops with a clear message if neither is set. Make sure the variable is set (e.g. as a CI secret) before running it:

export PYPI_TOKEN=pypi-...
invoke release.pypi

See Release.

docs.title: fix-python / fix-docstrings / fix-shell changed files I didn't expect
docs.text:
fix_* tasks modify files in place by design (see the naming convention). Always run them on a clean working tree so the diff is easy to review:

git status   # make sure everything is committed first
invoke format.fix-python
git diff     # review what changed

docs.title: My custom paths aren't picked up
docs.text: Only paths.* keys you explicitly set in invoke.yaml are used; unset ones fall back to their default, which is derived from other keys, not from a previous override. For example, setting paths.tests also moves the default for paths.unit_tests (since it's derived from paths.tests), but setting paths.unit_tests alone does not affect paths.tests. See Config → Overriding Paths for a worked example.

docs.title: Where do I ask for help / report a bug?
docs.text: Open an issue on GitHub. See the developer guide if you'd like to contribute a fix.

docs.title: Architecture and Design
docs.text: This document describes the internal architecture and design principles of invoke-tasklib.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
invoke-tasklib is designed around a simple idea: task modules are plain Invoke collections that share one config-resolution function. The core design follows these principles:

  1. One config entry point: every task reads project-specific values through invoke_tasklib.config.get_config, never directly from c.config.
  2. Convention over configuration: sensible defaults derived from package.name mean most projects only set one value (tasklib.package.name).
  3. Composability: the pre-built ns namespace is a convenience; any subset of task modules can be imported and combined with project-specific tasks.
  4. No hidden state: tasks only run external commands (ruff, pytest, uv, mike, ...); they don't maintain state between invocations.

docs.title: 1. Config Resolution
docs.text:
invoke_tasklib.config.get_config(c) is the single source of truth for project-specific values. It:

  • Reads the tasklib key from the Invoke config (c.config), which Invoke itself populates from invoke.yaml.
  • Merges it on top of DEFAULT_PACKAGE, DEFAULT_PATHS, DEFAULT_GROUPS and DEFAULT_TEST.
  • Rejects unknown keys and validates the values (package.python_version, package.import_name, groups.*, test.*).
  • Derives unset paths.* entries from package.import_name (for paths.src) or paths.tests (for the unit_tests/integration_tests/functional_tests/benchmarks entries).
  • Raises ValueError if package.name is missing, since nearly every task needs it, or if a value is invalid. Tasks call load_config, which turns the ValueError into an Exit.
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TasklibConfig:
    package: PackageConfig
    paths: PathsConfig
    groups: GroupsConfig
    test: TestConfig

Returning frozen dataclasses rather than a raw dict gives task authors static typing on cfg.package.name and similar accesses, and the values cannot be modified by a task.

docs.title: 2. Task Modules
docs.text:
Each task module (formatting.py, lint.py, imports.py, typecheck.py, testing.py, env.py, release.py, doc.py, security.py, clean.py, check.py) is a collection of @task-decorated functions. clean.py and check.py also have a default task (clean.all, check.all) that is run by invoke clean and invoke check. A module groups tasks that operate on the same underlying tool or concern (e.g. most of testing.py wraps pytest, except test.doctest-markdown, which wraps the standard library's doctest module directly).

Tasks that need project-specific values call load_config(c) at the top of the function body; tasks that don't (e.g. lint.check_python) skip it entirely.

docs.title: 3. The ns Namespace
docs.text:
invoke_tasklib/__init__.py has make_ns(*, exclude=(), include=None), which builds a new Collection by adding each task module (Collection.from_module(module, name=...)) as a sub-collection named after the module, leaving out the tasks of exclude and keeping only the tasks of include when it is set. The modules whose names would shadow the standard library or a builtin (format, types, test) are named formatting, typecheck and testing; the namespace names come from _MODULES, not from the module names. ns = make_ns() is the pre-built collection.

This is what gives consuming projects format.check-python, test.unit, etc. via a single from invoke_tasklib import ns in their tasks.py, or a trimmed copy with make_ns(...). A project that adds its own tasks should do it on its own make_ns() result, not on the shared ns.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
Here's how a task invocation flows through the system:

User runs `invoke test.unit --cov`
    ↓
Invoke loads invoke.yaml into c.config
    ↓
test.unit(c, cov=True) is called
    ↓
get_config(c) resolves package.name and paths.unit_tests
    ↓
Task builds the pytest command line
    ↓
c.run(cmd, pty=True) executes it as a subprocess

docs.title: Why a Shared get_config Instead of Per-Task Config?
docs.text:
Rationale: A single resolution function keeps defaults and the validation of the config in one place, and guarantees every task sees the same resolved paths (e.g. test.unit and types.check agree on package.name).

Trade-off: Every task pays the (cheap) cost of re-resolving config on each call, rather than resolving it once. This is negligible since get_config does no I/O beyond reading c.config.

docs.title: Why check_<target>/fix_<target> Naming?
docs.text:
Rationale: Makes the read-only/mutating counterpart of a task discoverable by name alone, and lets CI safely run every check_* task without risk of it modifying the working tree.

Trade-off: Slightly more verbose task names than a single format task with a --fix flag, but the split keeps invoke --list self-documenting.

docs.title: Why Frozen Dataclasses for Config?
docs.text:
Rationale: Static type checking (via ty) catches typos like cfg.path.src at development time, and attribute access reads better than nested keys, without requiring a runtime schema validation dependency.

Trade-off: The dataclasses don't validate values on construction; the validation is done by get_config (e.g. the package.name and package.python_version checks). It runs when a task starts, not when the collection is loaded, because the invoke.yaml values are only known once Invoke has built the context.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text: Tests use invoke.context.MockContext, which records every c.run(...) call without executing it. This lets tests assert on the exact shell command a task would run, without depending on ruff, pytest, uv, etc. being installed or configured in the test environment. The unit tests also patch shutil.which (an autouse fixture in tests/unit/conftest.py) so that the check of the PATH done by invoke_tasklib.runner.run passes on any machine.

docs.title: Future Directions
docs.text:
Potential areas for enhancement:

  1. Additional task modules for other common project needs (e.g. changelog generation).
  2. A task to validate a project's invoke.yaml against the config schema ahead of time (the errors of get_config are only raised when a task runs).

docs.title: Adding a New Task
docs.text:
1. Pick the right module (formatting.py, lint.py, imports.py, typecheck.py, testing.py, env.py, release.py, doc.py, security.py, clean.py or check.py), or create a new one if the task doesn't fit an existing namespace.
  2. Follow the check_<target>/fix_<target> naming convention when applicable (see Format).
  3. Call get_config(c) if the task needs project-specific paths or the package name, rather than hardcoding them.
  4. Write a docstring (Google style) describing the task; it is used both by invoke --list --help and by the reference docs.
  5. Add unit tests using invoke.context.MockContext (see existing tests for the pattern).
  6. If the module is new, register it in src/invoke_tasklib/__init__.py (_MODULES and __all__).
  7. Update the README task table and the corresponding user guide page.

docs.title: Testing Guidelines
docs.text:
Tests use invoke.context.MockContext to capture the shell commands a task would run, without actually running them. Each test module has two small helpers: _context builds a MockContext with an optional tasklib config, and _commands returns the commands passed to c.run (run=True makes MockContext record the calls in a Mock, hence the isinstance assertion):

from unittest.mock import Mock

from invoke.config import Config
from invoke.context import MockContext

from invoke_tasklib import lint


def _context(tasklib_config: dict | None = None) -> MockContext:
    overrides = {"tasklib": tasklib_config} if tasklib_config is not None else {}
    return MockContext(config=Config(overrides=overrides), run=True)


def _commands(c: MockContext) -> list[str]:
    run = c.run
    assert isinstance(run, Mock)
    return [call.args[0] for call in run.call_args_list]


def test_check_python() -> None:
    c = _context({"package": {"name": "mypkg"}})
    lint.check_python(c)
    assert _commands(c) == ["ruff check ."]

The tests/unit/conftest.py fixture makes every program look available on the PATH, so the unit tests do not depend on the tools installed on the machine. Tests that run the real tools go in tests/integration/.

docs.title: invoke_tasklib.config
docs.text:
Config resolution for invoke-tasklib tasks.

Consuming projects set project-specific values under a tasklib key in their invoke.yaml, e.g.::

tasklib:
  package:
    name: coola
  paths:
    docs_config: docs/mkdocs.yml

Only package.name (the distribution name) is required; everything else has a default derived from it. package.import_name defaults to the name with - replaced by _.

Return the defaults of the tasklib config section.

The defaults are registered with Invoke (see make_ns) so that the keys can also be set with the INVOKE_TASKLIB_<SECTION>_<KEY> environment variables, for example INVOKE_TASKLIB_PATHS_SRC. Invoke only reads an environment variable for a key that exists in the defaults.

A frozen dataclass with the resolved package, paths,

TasklibConfig

groups and test sections, each a frozen dataclass too,

TasklibConfig

e.g. cfg.paths.src.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If tasklib or one of its package, paths, groups and test sections is not a mapping, or if tasklib has a key that is not one of these sections, or if tasklib.package.name is not set or is not a string, or if a tasklib.paths value is not a non-empty string, or if tasklib.package.python_version is not a string such as "3.10" (an unquoted 3.10 is read by YAML as the float 3.1), or if tasklib.package.import_name is not a Python module name, or if a tasklib.groups value is neither a string nor a list of strings, or if the package, paths, groups or test section has an unknown key (for example a typo such as unit_test for unit_tests), or if a tasklib.test value is invalid (a timeout and cov_fail_under must be integers, with a timeout > 0 and cov_fail_under between 0 and 100, cov_reports must be report formats, and xdoctest must be a boolean).

>>> cfg = get_config(c)
>>> cfg.package.import_name
'mypkg'
>>> cfg.paths.src
'src/mypkg'
>>> cfg.groups

docs.title: Everyday Workflow
docs.text:
A typical local development loop looks like this:

invoke format.fix-python format.fix-docstrings   # auto-fix formatting
invoke lint.check-python imports.check-cycles types.check  # check quality
invoke test.unit --cov                            # run tests with coverage

And what CI typically runs (nothing should modify the working tree):

invoke format.check-python format.check-docstrings lint.check-python imports.check-cycles types.check
invoke test.all --cov

Since Invoke lets you chain multiple task names in one command, all of the above run as a single invoke call each.

docs.title: Passing Arguments to the Tools
docs.text:
The tasks that run pytest (test.all, test.unit, test.integration, test.functional), ruff (format.check-python, format.fix-python, lint.check-python, lint.fix-python), docformatter (format.check-docstrings, format.fix-docstrings) and ty (types.check) have two options:

  • --args adds arguments to the command. The value is one string, split like a shell does.
  • --paths runs the tool on these files or directories instead of the default ones (the project for ruff, paths.src for docformatter, the scope directory for pytest).
invoke test.unit --args "-k foo -x" --paths tests/unit/test_foo.py
invoke lint.check-python --args "--select E" --paths "src/a.py src/b.py"
invoke format.check-python --paths src/a.py

For types.check, --args goes to ty only and --paths goes to ty and pyright. The arguments and the paths are quoted, so they are never interpreted by the shell.

docs.title: External Tools
docs.text:
Tasks are thin wrappers around external command-line tools. Each is expected to be available on PATH (or installed via env.install/env.create-venv):

Tool Used by ruff format.check-python, format.fix-python, lint.check-python docformatter format.check-docstrings, format.fix-docstrings shellcheck format.check-shell shfmt format.fix-shell ty types.check pytest test.* except test.doctest and test.doctest-markdown pytest-timeout test.unit, test.integration, test.functional, test.all pytest-cov the --cov option of the test.* tasks coverage test.coverage-report xdoctest test.* (unless test.xdoctest is false), test.doctest-src pytest-benchmark test.benchmark uv env.*, release.* twine (via uvx) release.build --check codespell lint.check-spelling pre-commit lint.pre-commit mkdocs doc.build, doc.serve mike doc.publish-dev, doc.publish-latest git doc.publish-latest pip-audit (via uv run) security.audit

Most of these come from your project's own dev/docs dependency groups; see Env for how env.install wires them up, and the Troubleshooting guide if a task fails with a "command not found" error.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke check

Runs, in this order, and stops at the first failure:

  1. format.check-python
  2. format.check-docstrings
  3. lint.check-python
  4. types.check
  5. imports.check-cycles
  6. test.unit

None of them modifies a file. Use the tasks directly (with --args and --paths) to run only one of them, or lint.pre-commit to run the hooks of the project. To leave check out of a collection, use make_ns(exclude=["check"]).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Task Behavior clean.all Removes build artifacts and caches from the repo root clean.pycache Removes all __pycache__ directories

clean.all is the default task of the clean namespace, so invoke clean runs it.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke clean

Removes, if present, at the repository root:

  • Directories: build, dist, .pytest_cache, .ruff_cache, .coverage_html, htmlcov, .benchmarks, .mypy_cache, .tox, .nox, .hypothesis, and site only if the project has a mkdocs.yml or docs/mkdocs.yml file (what produces it)
  • Glob-matched directories: *.egg-info (at the root and in src) and every __pycache__ directory of the project. The .venv, .git, .pytest_cache and node_modules directories are never walked into, so nothing inside them is removed.
  • Files: .coverage, .coverage.* (parallel coverage data), coverage.xml

Nothing is removed if the corresponding directory or file doesn't exist, so clean is safe to run repeatedly (it's idempotent) and doesn't fail on an already-clean checkout. A symbolic link to a directory is removed as a link, and the directory it points to is left untouched.

To remove only the __pycache__ directories:

invoke clean.pycache

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
This page describes the invoke_tasklib.config module, which resolves the shared config that all invoke-tasklib tasks read from.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python and Invoke.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every task in invoke-tasklib calls load_config(c) (get_config(c) with a clean exit on an invalid config, see below) to read project-specific values from an invoke.yaml at the root of the consuming project, under a tasklib key:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package
    python_version: "3.14"
  paths:
    src: src/my_package
    tests: tests
    unit_tests: tests/unit
    integration_tests: tests/integration
    functional_tests: tests/functional
    benchmarks: tests/benchmarks
    docs_config: docs/mkdocs.yml
  groups:
    install: dev
    update: dev,docs

Only tasklib.package.name (the distribution name, as on PyPI) is required. Everything else has a default, and most of the paths defaults are derived from package.name or from paths.tests.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Key Default package.import_name <package.name> with - replaced by _ package.python_version "3.14" paths.src src/<package.import_name>, or <package.import_name> if only that directory exists paths.tests tests paths.unit_tests <paths.tests>/unit paths.integration_tests <paths.tests>/integration paths.functional_tests <paths.tests>/functional paths.benchmarks <paths.tests>/benchmarks paths.docs_config docs/mkdocs.yml groups.install dev groups.update dev,docs test.unit_timeout 10 test.integration_timeout 60 test.functional_timeout 60 test.xdoctest true test.cov_fail_under not set test.cov_reports html,xml,term

The test section sets the per-test timeout in seconds of each test scope, whether pytest runs with --xdoctest (it requires the xdoctest package, so set xdoctest: false if the project does not have it), and a coverage threshold: with --cov, cov_fail_under is forwarded as --cov-fail-under. Timeouts and cov_fail_under are integers, xdoctest is a boolean. cov_reports is a comma-separated string or a list of the --cov-report formats of pytest-cov (html, xml, json, lcov, annotate, term, term-missing) that --cov generates. An empty value passes no --cov-report, so pytest-cov uses its default.

package.import_name is the name used to import the package. It is used by imports.check-cycles, release.build (the import check of the built artifacts) and the --cov option of the test tasks. Set it when it is not the distribution name with - replaced by _. It must be a Python module name.

If tasklib.package.name is missing, get_config raises a ValueError; the tasks use load_config, which turns it into an invoke.exceptions.Exit with the same message and the exit code 2 (no traceback).

Unknown keys in tasklib itself (typically a typo of a section such as path) and in the package, paths, groups or test sections (such as paths.unit_test) also raise a ValueError that lists the valid keys and suggests the closest one, instead of being silently ignored. Each section must be a mapping, package.name and every paths.* value must be a non-empty string, and test.cov_fail_under must be between 0 and 100.

package.python_version must be a quoted string such as "3.10" or "3.10.4". YAML reads an unquoted 3.10 as the number 3.1, so get_config raises a ValueError for any non-string or malformed value instead of silently creating a virtual environment with the wrong Python.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Every key can also be set with an INVOKE_TASKLIB_<SECTION>_<KEY> environment variable, for example INVOKE_TASKLIB_PATHS_SRC=lib or INVOKE_TASKLIB_TEST_UNIT_TIMEOUT=30. This is handy in CI. It works because make_ns (and so ns) registers the defaults of the tasklib section with Invoke, which only reads the environment variables of the keys that it knows. The usual Invoke order applies: the environment variables win over invoke.yaml.

Invoke reads an environment variable as a string and converts it to the type of the default value: an integer for the timeouts, and, for a boolean such as INVOKE_TASKLIB_TEST_XDOCTEST, 0 or an empty value is false and anything else (including false) is true. test.cov_fail_under accepts a string of digits. A collection built by hand (Collection(lint, ...)) has no defaults, so it does not read the environment variables unless you call ns.configure({"tasklib": invoke_tasklib.config.default_config()}).

docs.title: Minimal Config
docs.text:
The smallest valid invoke.yaml only sets the package name:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

With this, paths.src resolves to src/my_package, paths.unit_tests resolves to tests/unit, and so on.

docs.title: Overriding Paths
docs.text:
Override any individual path without affecting the others' defaults, for example when tests live outside tests/:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package
  paths:
    tests: test
    benchmarks: test/perf

Here paths.unit_tests still resolves to <paths.tests>/unit, i.e. test/unit, since it is derived from the overridden paths.tests.

docs.title: Overriding Dependency Groups
docs.text:
env.install and env.update install uv dependency groups by name. Projects that define more groups than dev/docs (e.g. test, lint) can change the defaults those tasks use, instead of passing --groups on every invocation:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package
  groups:
    install: dev,test
    update: dev,test,docs

Each value can also be written as a YAML list, which is joined with commas:

tasklib:
  groups:
    install: [dev, test]
    update: [dev, test, docs]

The --groups flag of the tasks stays a comma-separated string (--groups dev,docs).

docs.title: Using get_config in a Custom Task
docs.text:
get_config returns frozen dataclasses (cfg.package, cfg.paths, cfg.groups, cfg.test), so the values are read as attributes and cannot be modified. It raises a ValueError on an invalid config; use load_config in a task to exit with a message instead. get_config is the same function every built-in task uses, so a project-specific task can read the same config:

from invoke.tasks import task
from invoke_tasklib.config import get_config


@task
def my_task(c):
    cfg = get_config(c)
    print(cfg.package.name, cfg.paths.src)

docs.title: Doc
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.doc module, which provides tasks to publish versioned documentation with mike, on top of MkDocs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Task Behavior doc.build Builds the docs, failing on warnings doc.serve Serves the docs locally doc.publish-dev Publishes development (unstable) docs doc.publish-latest Publishes latest (stable) docs

Both tasks read paths.docs_config from the resolved config (default: docs/mkdocs.yml) and pass it to mike via --config-file.

docs.title: Publishing Development Docs
docs.text:
invoke doc.publish-dev

Deploys the current docs under the main version with the dev alias (mike deploy replaces an existing main version, so it is not deleted first), then pushes to the configured remote (typically gh-pages). Pass --no-push to only commit the docs branch locally.

docs.title: Publishing Latest (Stable) Docs
docs.text:
invoke doc.publish-latest

Determines the version to publish from the most recent git version tag (a tag like v1.2.3, read with git tag --list 'v[0-9]*' --sort=-v:refname), truncated to <major>.<minor> (e.g. 1.2). It then deploys the current docs under that tag with the latest alias, and sets latest as the default version shown to visitors. Pass --no-push to only commit the docs branch locally.

To publish a specific version without looking at the git tags, pass it explicitly:

invoke doc.publish-latest --version 1.2

The task fails if there is no version tag and no --version, because publishing under a made-up version would be a setup error. Pre-release versions (1.2.0rc1, 1.2.0a1, 1.2.0.dev1, ...) are skipped, so they never become latest.

The task also refuses to move latest backwards: if a newer <major>.<minor> is already published (mike list --json), for example when releasing a 1.1.5 backport after 1.2.0, it fails with Refusing to publish 1.1 as latest. Pass --force to publish the older version anyway.

docs.title: Local Preview
docs.text:
The publishing tasks are meant for CI (they --push to the remote). To check and preview docs locally:

invoke doc.build
invoke doc.serve

doc.build runs mkdocs build --strict, so a broken link or a missing reference fails the task (unlike a mike deploy into a throw-away branch, which does not). doc.serve runs mkdocs serve with live reload. Both use paths.docs_config and need the docs dependency group.

docs.title: Env
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.env module, which provides tasks to set up and inspect a project's Python environment using uv.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Task Behavior env.create-venv Creates a virtual environment and installs invoke env.install Installs project dependencies and the package (editable) env.update Updates dependencies and pre-commit hooks env.show-installed-packages Shows the installed packages env.show-python-config Shows the Python configuration

docs.title: Creating a Virtual Environment
docs.text:
invoke env.create-venv

Creates (or recreates) a .venv using the package.python_version from the resolved config, and installs invoke into it with uv pip install invoke. The task is run with invoke, so invoke must already be available (for example through uv tool install invoke) to run it.

Warning

This clears any existing .venv.

docs.title: Installing Dependencies
docs.text:
invoke env.install

Runs uv sync --locked, which also installs the package itself in editable mode. --locked fails if uv.lock is out of date with pyproject.toml instead of silently using it (run uv lock to refresh it).

Flag Default Adds to uv sync --optional-deps on --all-extras --groups groups.install (default dev) --group <name> for each comma-separated group

--groups takes a comma-separated list of dependency groups to install, e.g. dev,docs. Pass an empty string to skip installing any group.

Disable the on-by-default optional deps, or override the groups, with:

invoke env.install --no-optional-deps --groups ""
invoke env.install --groups dev,docs

The default value of --groups comes from the resolved config's groups.install ("dev" unless overridden in invoke.yaml), so a project with more groups than dev/docs can change the default once instead of passing --groups on every call.

docs.title: Updating Dependencies
docs.text:
invoke env.update

Runs uv lock --upgrade, updates the pre-commit hooks (pre-commit autoupdate, only if the project has a .pre-commit-config.yaml file), and reinstalls the project with the groups from --groups (default: the resolved config's groups.update, "dev,docs" unless overridden).

invoke env.update --groups dev,docs,test

Warning

Updating dependencies may introduce breaking changes. Review the changes and run the test suite afterward.

docs.title: Inspecting the Environment
docs.text:
invoke env.show-installed-packages
invoke env.show-python-config

env.show-python-config prints the installed Python versions known to uv, the interpreter uv would select, and the interpreter currently on PATH. It does not fail when no python is on the PATH.

docs.title: Format
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.formatting module, which provides tasks for checking and fixing code, docstring, and shell script formatting.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Tasks follow a check_<target> / fix_<target> naming convention:

  • check_<target> tasks are read-only: they fail with a non-zero exit code if formatting is wrong, but never modify files.
  • fix_<target> tasks modify files in place to match the expected format.
Task Behavior format.check-python Checks Python formatting with ruff (read-only) format.fix-python Formats Python code with ruff (in place) format.check-docstrings Checks docstring formatting with docformatter (read-only) format.fix-docstrings Formats docstrings with docformatter (in place) format.check-shell Checks shell scripts with shellcheck (read-only) format.fix-shell Formats shell scripts with shfmt (in place)

docs.title: Checking Format
docs.text:
invoke format.check-python
invoke format.check-docstrings
invoke format.check-shell

These are safe to run anywhere, including in CI, since they never modify files.

docs.title: Fixing Format
docs.text:
invoke format.fix-python
invoke format.fix-docstrings
invoke format.fix-shell

Warning

fix_* tasks modify files in place. Ensure your work is committed before running them.

docs.title: Docstring Style
docs.text: format.check-docstrings and format.fix-docstrings run docformatter against paths.src from the resolved config, using the [tool.docformatter] section of the consuming project's pyproject.toml (via --config ./pyproject.toml).

docs.title: Shell Scripts
docs.text:
format.check-shell and format.fix-shell operate on every *.sh file in the project. The .git, .venv, .pytest_cache, node_modules, build, dist and site directories are not searched, so third-party scripts (for example the activation scripts of a virtual environment) are never checked or rewritten.

Note

shellcheck and shfmt are not Python packages, so they aren't installed by env.install. Install them with your system package manager, e.g. brew install shellcheck shfmt on macOS or apt install shellcheck on Debian/Ubuntu (shfmt there comes from the golang-go toolchain or a release binary).

docs.title: Imports
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.imports module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Task Behavior imports.check-cycles Checks for cyclic import dependencies by importing each module in isolation (read-only)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke imports.check-cycles

This discovers every module of package.name (from the resolved config): the package itself, its subpackages and all the modules, recursively (__main__ modules are skipped). The discovery walks the package directories and does not import anything, so it cannot fail with the cycle it is meant to detect. Each module is then imported in its own python -c process, using the interpreter that runs Invoke. Importing a module in isolation fails if it depends on something that is only initialized as a side effect of importing a sibling or parent module first, which is the usual symptom of a cyclic import dependency. For example, two sibling modules that do from pkg.b import y and from pkg.a import x are reported even though neither is a package.

docs.title: Lint
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.lint module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Task Behavior lint.check-python Checks code linting with ruff (read-only) lint.fix-python Fixes auto-fixable linting issues in place with ruff lint.check-spelling Checks the spelling with codespell (read-only) lint.pre-commit Runs all the pre-commit hooks on all the files

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke lint.check-python

This runs ruff check .. In GitHub Actions (GITHUB_ACTIONS=true) it adds --output-format=github, so ruff annotates violations directly on the diff; locally the readable default output is used. Pass --output-format to choose the format explicitly:

invoke lint.check-python --output-format=concise

invoke lint.fix-python

This runs ruff check --fix ., which rewrites files in place for every auto-fixable violation. Not every lint rule is auto-fixable, so lint.check-python may still report violations afterwards that need a manual fix.

Warning

lint.fix-python modifies files in place. Commit your work before running it.

docs.title: Spelling and Pre-commit Hooks
docs.text:
invoke lint.check-spelling

This runs codespell . (the configuration is read from pyproject.toml). --args and --paths work as for the other tasks.

invoke lint.pre-commit

This runs pre-commit run --all-files. Pass --args to select a hook, e.g. --args ruff-format. The hooks may modify files.

docs.title: Release
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.release module, which provides tasks to build and publish the package to PyPI using uv.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Task Behavior release.build Builds the package and verifies installation (--check also validates metadata with twine) release.pypi Builds and publishes the package to PyPI

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
invoke release.build

Runs uv build, then verifies the artifacts it produced: the newest wheel and the newest source distribution in dist/ are each installed in an isolated uv run environment (uv run --isolated --no-project --with dist/<file>) and the package is imported from it. The task fails if the build did not produce a wheel or a source distribution.

Pass --check to additionally validate the package's PyPI metadata with twine check:

invoke release.build --check

docs.title: Publishing to PyPI
docs.text:
invoke release.pypi

Builds the package (via release.build, which clears dist/ first so stale artifacts are never uploaded) and then runs uv publish. The token is read from the PYPI_TOKEN environment variable (or UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN) and handed to uv publish through its environment, so it never appears on the command line. The task fails before building if no token is set.

release.pypi is the token-based way to publish, for example from a local machine. It is not the only one: a CI workflow can build the package with release.build and publish it with PyPI Trusted Publishing (OpenID Connect), which needs no token at all. This repository releases that way (see .github/workflows/release-pypi.yaml), and does not use release.pypi.

Warning

This publishes a new version to PyPI, which cannot be undone. Make sure PYPI_TOKEN is set and that you are releasing the intended version before running this task.

invoke security.audit

This runs uv run pip-audit, which checks the currently installed dependencies against known vulnerability databases (via PyPI's Advisory Database) and exits non-zero if any known vulnerability is found.

Since it audits installed packages, run env.install first if dependencies haven't been installed yet.

docs.title: Test
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.testing module, which provides tasks to run doctests, unit/integration/functional tests, and benchmarks with pytest.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Task Behavior test.doctest Runs doctests on source code and markdown files test.doctest-src Runs doctests on source code test.doctest-markdown Runs doctests on Python examples in markdown files test.unit Runs unit tests test.integration Runs integration tests test.functional Runs functional tests test.all Runs all tests (unit, integration, and functional) test.coverage-report Generates an HTML/terminal report from existing coverage data test.benchmark Runs performance benchmarks

All test tasks (except test.benchmark, test.doctest, and test.doctest-markdown) run pytest with --xdoctest enabled, so doctests embedded in the code under test are also collected. Set tasklib.test.xdoctest: false if the project does not have the xdoctest package.

docs.title: Running Doctests
docs.text:
invoke test.doctest

Runs both test.doctest-src and test.doctest-markdown.

invoke test.doctest-src

Runs doctests against paths.src from the resolved config.

invoke test.doctest-markdown

Recursively finds every *.md file in the project (skipping .venv, .pytest_cache, .git, and node_modules) and runs, for each one:

python -m doctest -o NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE -o ELLIPSIS -o REPORT_NDIFF <file>.md

so Python code examples embedded in markdown files (README, docs, ...) stay correct and up to date. NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE and ELLIPSIS make output comparisons more forgiving (whitespace differences are ignored, and ... in expected output matches any text), and REPORT_NDIFF gives a readable diff when an example's output doesn't match. A markdown file with no >>> doctest blocks is still visited but simply reports zero tests, so it always "passes".

docs.title: Running Tests by Scope
docs.text:
invoke test.unit
invoke test.integration
invoke test.functional

Each targets its own path (paths.unit_tests, paths.integration_tests, paths.functional_tests), with a longer default timeout (60s vs 10s) for integration and functional tests, since they typically exercise more of the system. The timeouts are the test.unit_timeout, test.integration_timeout and test.functional_timeout values of the config. If the directory of test.integration or test.functional does not exist, the task prints a message and skips it instead of failing with a pytest error. test.unit does the same, except that when paths.unit_tests does not exist but paths.tests does (a flat tests/ layout), it runs the whole paths.tests directory.

invoke test.all

Runs everything in paths.tests in a single pytest invocation, with the largest of the three timeouts (60s by default, since the integration and functional tests are part of that directory).

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Pass --cov to test.unit, test.integration, test.functional, or test.all to generate coverage reports. The formats are the test.cov_reports value of the config (html,xml,term by default, each one is a --cov-report of pytest-cov; an empty value leaves the choice to pytest-cov):

invoke test.unit --cov

test.integration --cov and test.functional --cov append to any existing coverage data (--cov-append), so they compose with a prior test.unit --cov run to build up combined coverage across scopes:

invoke test.unit --cov
invoke test.integration --cov
invoke test.functional --cov

If tasklib.test.cov_fail_under is set, it is passed as --cov-fail-under and the task fails when the coverage is lower. Since the integration and functional tasks append to the existing data, run test.unit --cov first (it replaces the data) or coverage erase, otherwise the result depends on what was run before.

invoke test.coverage-report

Runs python -m coverage (the interpreter of the tests) to regenerate the HTML report and prints the terminal summary from whatever coverage data (.coverage) is currently on disk — the data produced by an earlier --cov run — without re-running the tests. Pass --open-browser to also open htmlcov/index.html in your default browser:

invoke test.coverage-report --open-browser

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
invoke test.benchmark

Runs pytest --benchmark-only against paths.benchmarks. This requires pytest-benchmark to be installed. The task is skipped with a message if paths.benchmarks does not exist.
